{{Short description|Physical theorem in special relativity}}
In [[classical mechanics]], the '''no-interaction theorem''' is a [[no-go theorem]] that shows that a system of many interacting particles cannot exist when [[special relativity]] is taken into account. It concludes that the only allowed configuration is that of a system of [[free particle]]s only. The theorem is important for [[modern physics]], as it suggest the necessity of introducing [[field (physics)|fields]] to describe interactions between particles. This theorem excludes the possibility of [[action at a distance]]. The modern understanding of the [[Fundamental interaction|fundamental interactions]] ([[gravity]], [[electromagnetism]] and [[Nuclear force|nuclear forces]]) is that objects can interact by locally perturbing the fields in which each interaction propagates.

Various formulations of the theorem exist. The earliest version was given by Douglas G. Currie, Thomas F. Jordan and [[E. C. George Sudarshan]] in 1963,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Currie |first=D. G. |last2=Jordan |first2=T. F. |last3=Sudarshan |first3=E. C. G. |date=1963-04-01 |title=Relativistic Invariance and Hamiltonian Theories of Interacting Particles |url=https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.35.350 |journal=Reviews of Modern Physics |language=en-US |volume=35 |issue=2 |pages=350–375 |doi=10.1103/RevModPhys.35.350 |issn=0034-6861 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260208215400/https://journals.aps.org/rmp/abstract/10.1103/RevModPhys.35.350 |archive-date=2026-02-08}}</ref> extended by John T. Cannon and Jordan in 1964,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cannon |first=John T. |last2=Jordan |first2=Thomas F. |date=1964-03-01 |title=A No-Interaction Theorem in Classical Relativistic Hamiltonian Particle Dynamics |url=https://pubs.aip.org/jmp/article/5/3/299/230851/A-No-Interaction-Theorem-in-Classical-Relativistic |journal=Journal of Mathematical Physics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=299–307 |doi=10.1063/1.1704121 |issn=0022-2488|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and generalized by [[Heinrich Leutwyler]] in 1965.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Leutwyler |first=H. |date=1965-05-01 |title=A no-interaction theorem in classical relativistic Hamiltonian particle mechanics |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02749856 |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento (1955-1965) |language=en |volume=37 |issue=2 |pages=556–567 |doi=10.1007/BF02749856 |issn=1827-6121|url-access=subscription }}</ref> An alternative formulation was given by Hendrik van Dam and [[Eugene Wigner]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Van Dam |first=H. |last2=Wigner |first2=E. P. |date=1965-06-21 |title=Classical Relativistic Mechanics of Interacting Point Particles |url=https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.138.B1576 |journal=Physical Review |language=en-US |volume=138 |issue=6B |pages=B1576–B1582 |doi=10.1103/PhysRev.138.B1576 |issn=0031-899X |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240712124339/https://journals.aps.org/pr/abstract/10.1103/PhysRev.138.B1576 |archive-date=2024-07-12}}</ref> in 1966.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Marmo |first=G. |last2=Samuel |first2=J. |last3=Simoni |first3=A. |last4=Zaccaria |first4=F. |date=1988-10-01 |title=No-interaction theorem for classical relativistic particles with Grassmann internal coordinates |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02789492 |journal=Il Nuovo Cimento A (1965-1970) |language=en |volume=100 |issue=4 |pages=447–461 |doi=10.1007/BF02789492 |issn=1826-9869|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Williams |first=Anthony G. |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/Introduction_to_Quantum_Field_Theory/o7x8EAAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=no+interaction+theorem+l+field+theory&pg=PA156&printsec=frontcover |title=Introduction to Quantum Field Theory: Classical Mechanics to Gauge Field Theories |date=2022-08-04 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-108-60087-3 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Ohanian |first=Hans C. |url=http://archive.org/details/gravitationspace0000ohan |title=Gravitation and spacetime |date=1976 |publisher=New York : Norton |others=Internet Archive |isbn=978-0-393-09198-4}}</ref>

== Assumptions ==
Consider a system with a finite number ''N'' of particles described by [[special relativity]] using [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangian]] or [[Hamiltonian mechanics]]. The no-interaction theorem states that, aside from [[Contact force|contact forces]], there can be no direct interaction between any two particles in a form that is manifestly invariant under [[Lorentz transformation|Lorentz transformations]] (covariant).<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Goldstein |first=Herbert |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/Classical_Mechanics/tJCuQgAACAAJ?hl=en |title=Classical Mechanics |last2=Poole |first2=Charles P. |last3=Safko |first3=John L. |date=2002 |publisher=Addison Wesley |isbn=978-0-201-65702-9 |language=en}}</ref> The theorem can be explicitly shown using three postulates:

# Conservation of total linear momentum: the total [[four-momentum]] at a given time <math display="inline">t</math> is expressed as  <math display="inline">P^\mu(t)=\sum_{a=1}^N P_{(a)}^\mu(t)</math>, where <math display="inline">P_{(a)}^\mu(t)</math> is the four-momentum of particle <math display="inline">a</math>. The postulate assumes that <math display="inline">P^\mu(t)=\text{constant}</math> at any time.
# No coincidence: there are no two distinct particles <math display="inline">a</math> and <math display="inline">b</math> with proper times <math display="inline">t_a,t_b</math> such that <math display="inline">P_{(a)}^\mu(t_a)=P_{(b)}^\mu(t_b)</math>.
# Asymptotically straight [[World line|world lines]]: for large times, <math display="inline">t_a\to \pm \infty</math>, <math display="inline">P_{(a)}^\mu(t_a)\to \text{constant}</math> .

which leads to the momentum of individual particles being constant (no interactions) at any time. The third postulate implies that the total momentum transforms under [[Lorentz transformation|Lorentz transformations]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite book |last=Mann |first=Ronald A. |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/The_Classical_Dynamics_of_Particles/gsg3BQAAQBAJ?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=no+interaction+theorem+currie&pg=PA187&printsec=frontcover |title=The Classical Dynamics of Particles: Galilean and Lorentz Relativity |date=2013-10-22 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-1-4832-6201-7 |language=en}}</ref> 

More advanced proofs rely on [[Group theory|group theoretical]] arguments.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Esposito |first=Giampiero |url=https://www.google.fr/books/edition/From_Classical_to_Quantum_Mechanics/STGH8fuDhe0C?hl=en&gbpv=1&dq=leutwyler+no+interaction+theorem&pg=PA556&printsec=frontcover |title=From Classical to Quantum Mechanics: An Introduction to the Formalism, Foundations and Applications |last2=Marmo |first2=Giuseppe |last3=Sudarshan |first3=George |date=2004-03-11 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-1-139-45054-6 |language=en}}</ref><ref name=":2" />

== Case of two identical particles ==
The no-interaction theorem indicates that two classical particles of mass <math>m</math> cannot interact. If <math display="inline">u^\mu_{(1)}</math> is the [[four-velocity]] of particle 1 and <math display="inline">u^\mu_{(2)}</math> the four-velocity of particle 2, the total momentum is<ref name=":1" /><math display="block">P^\mu=mu_{(1)}^\mu+mu_{(2)}^\mu.</math>In another frame, the four-momentum transforms as<math display="block">P'^\mu=a^{\mu}{}_\nu P^\nu</math>for some Lorentz boost <math display="inline">a^\mu{}_\nu</math>.

Van Dam and Wigner [[Proof by contradiction|prove by contradiction]] that momentum is not conserved unless the particles come into contact.<ref name=":1" /> Supposing particle 1 is at point ''P'' at time <math display="inline">t=0</math> and also at point ''P'' at time <math display="inline">t'=0</math> (following its world line), and particle 2 is at point ''Q'' at <math display="inline">t=0</math> and at ''Q''' at <math display="inline">t'=0</math>, the transformation of the total momentum is given by 
<math display="block">mu_{(1)}^{\prime\mu}|_P+mu_{(2)}^{\prime\mu}|_Q=a^{\mu}{}_\nu \left(mu_{(1)}^\nu|_P+mu_{(2)}^\nu |_{Q'}\right),</math>
but as the four-velocity at point ''P'' also transforms as 
<math display="block">u_{(1)}^{\prime\mu}|_P=a^{\mu}{}_\nu u_{(1)}^\nu|_P,</math>
and at point ''Q'' as
<math display="block">u_{(2)}^{\prime\mu}|_Q=a^{\mu}{}_\nu u_{(2)}^\nu|_Q,</math>as <math display="inline">a^\mu{}_\nu</math> is arbitrary we conclude that <math display="block">u_{(2)}^{\mu}|_{Q'}= u_{(2)}^\mu|_Q,</math>meaning that the velocity of  particle 2 remains constant when moving from ''Q'' to ''Q'''. This result implies that the momentum of each particle remains constant, which would be the case if the particles did not interact.
